0.title: When People Clash
0.essay:
A tense silence at the dinner table. An email from your manager that makes your stomach drop. A church meeting where voices rise and someone walks out. Conflict is part of every life, and most of us handle it badly. If you dread hard conversations, or keep having the same argument, this study is for you.

Two ways to get it wrong

When people clash, most of us reach for one of two reflexes. Some of us run: we avoid, go quiet, smooth things over and pretend all is well. Others of us fight: we argue to win, raise our voices, gather allies and keep score. Neither brings real peace.

Scripture offers a third way. It is not a technique but a person. God himself faced the deepest conflict there has ever been, the rebellion of his creatures, and he did not run from it or crush us in it. He came to us in his Son and made peace “by the blood of his cross” (Colossians 1:20). Those who have received that peace are called to carry it into their homes, offices and churches. “Blessed are the peacemakers” (Matthew 5:9).

Where we are going

We will look honestly at where conflict comes from, why we run or fight, and what lies underneath. Then we will see the God who made peace, learn the peacemaker’s way from Jesus, Proverbs and Paul, and end with practical wisdom for the hard conversation itself.

This study is about the conflict while it is happening. What comes after, forgiving, rebuilding trust and walking the long road of reconciliation, is the subject of the study Forgiveness & Reconciliation. The study The Tongue says more about our words, and the study Anger about the heat we bring into a quarrel.

The chapters

Where Peace Breaks Down; Running Away and Hitting Back; What Lies Beneath the Quarrel; The God Who Came to Make Peace; The Peacemaker’s Way; and Before, During and After the Hard Conversation.

For reflection

Think of the last real conflict you were part of. Did you tend to run from it or to fight it? What did you most want in that moment?

1.title: Where Peace Breaks Down
1.essay:
It might be the washing-up, or the budget, or who said what at the family wedding. It might be a colleague who takes credit for your work, a boss who changes the plan without asking, or a church member who seems to oppose every idea you have. Conflict comes in all sizes, and it seems to find us wherever we go.

At home, at work and at church

At home, conflict is close and constant. Husbands and wives disagree about money, children, in-laws and how to spend Saturday. Parents and teenagers clash over phones and curfews. Adult brothers and sisters fall out over a parent’s care or a will. Because we love these people, the wounds go deep.

At work, conflict is often about power. Someone has authority over you, or wants it. There are deadlines, limited budgets and unclear roles. You may spend more hours with a difficult colleague than with your own family, and you cannot simply walk away.

At church, conflict can feel the most painful of all, because it should not happen there. Yet churches argue about music, buildings, decisions, leadership and a hundred small things. And people who have been hurt in church sometimes stop going altogether.

Not new

The Bible is honest about this. In the early chapters of Genesis, brothers quarrel and one kills the other. Later, the herdsmen of Abram and his nephew Lot came to blows over grazing land. Abram did something remarkable: “Let there be no strife between you and me, and between your herdsmen and my herdsmen, for we are kinsmen” (Genesis 13:8). He was the senior man, yet he let Lot choose first. We will come back to that kind of generosity.

Even the first church had a quarrel within months of Pentecost. “A complaint by the Hellenists arose against the Hebrews because their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution” (Acts 6:1). The complaint was fair. The apostles did not dismiss it or take offence. They listened, gathered the church and appointed seven men to put it right, and every one of the seven had a Greek name. Handled well, a conflict made the church stronger.

Two good men, one sharp quarrel

Then there are Paul and Barnabas. They had travelled together, suffered together and seen churches born. As they planned a second journey, Barnabas wanted to take his cousin John Mark, who had left them part-way through the first. Paul refused, because Mark “had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia and had not gone with them to the work” (Acts 15:38). “And there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other” (Acts 15:39).

Who was right? Luke does not say. Barnabas, whose name means “son of encouragement” (Acts 4:36), saw a young man who needed a second chance. Paul saw a hard mission that needed people who would stay the course. Both cared about the gospel. Many of our conflicts are like this: not good against evil, but two good concerns pulling in different directions, held by two people who both feel they are protecting something precious. Recognising that is often the first step towards peace.

Two women Paul loved

In his warmest letter, Paul turns from calling the Philippians “my joy and crown” (Philippians 4:1) to a painful matter. “I entreat Euodia and I entreat Syntyche to agree in the Lord” (Philippians 4:2). These were not troublemakers. They had “labored side by side with me in the gospel” (Philippians 4:3). Paul does not take sides, and he does not tell them to pretend. He asks them to find a common mind “in the Lord”, on the ground they already share. And he asks a trusted friend to help them, as we will see.

Imagine how it felt when this letter was read aloud in church. Their quarrel had become everyone’s concern. Unresolved conflict rarely stays private for long.

Is all conflict sin?

No. People differ in temperament, background and judgment. Some disagreements are simply part of living as finite creatures who see from different places. Some are necessary: a wrong must be named, a decision challenged, an injustice resisted. Jesus himself caused a great deal of conflict. The question is not whether we will face conflict, but whether we will handle it in a way that honours God, serves the other person and makes us more like Christ. Seen that way, even a painful clash can become an opportunity.

Difficult people

Some people really are difficult. They are prickly, controlling, critical or simply very different from us. The psalmist knew this: “I am for peace, but when I speak, they are for war!” (Psalm 120:7). This study will not pretend that every conflict can be solved by a good conversation. But it will ask us to look first at the one person we can change.

An example

Two volunteers run the youth group at a small church. One loves planning; the other loves spontaneity. Over a year, small irritations grow into a cold war. Each complains about the other to their spouse, and soon to a few friends. Neither has said a word to the other directly. The young people can feel the tension, though nobody has explained it.

For reflection

Where do you face the most conflict at the moment: at home, at work, at church or elsewhere? Think of a recent disagreement. Could it be two good concerns pulling in different directions? What do you think Paul meant by asking Euodia and Syntyche to “agree in the Lord”? Is there a conflict you have been treating as everyone else’s problem?

2.title: Running Away and Hitting Back
2.essay:
When conflict comes, most of us have a reflex, learned early and repeated for years. Some of us run. Some of us fight. Both feel natural, and both feel justified at the time. But neither leads to peace.

Running away

The first reflex is escape. It has many forms. We avoid the person, change the subject or leave the room. We say “It’s fine” when it is not. We go quiet for days. We agree to anything to make the tension stop. We stop going to the small group, change churches, or simply let a friendship die without a word.

This can look like peace. In fact it is often peace-faking. God rebuked the false prophets of Jeremiah’s day because “They have healed the wound of my people lightly, saying, ‘Peace, peace,’ when there is no peace” (Jeremiah 6:14). A wound covered with a plaster but never cleaned does not heal. It festers.

Escape also has a sideways form: we talk about the problem to everyone except the person concerned. We vent to a spouse, hint to friends, or share a “prayer request” that is really a complaint. Proverbs puts it plainly: “For lack of wood the fire goes out, and where there is no whisperer, quarreling ceases” (Proverbs 26:20). Avoiding the person while talking about them only feeds the fire.

Jacob fled from his brother Esau’s anger, meaning to stay away “a while” (Genesis 27:44). It was twenty years before they met again. Running rarely takes as short a time as we hope.

Hitting back

The second reflex is attack. Again it has many forms. We argue to win, not to understand. We interrupt, raise our voice, use sarcasm or the cutting remark we know will land. We bring up the past: “You always…”, “You never…”. We blame, as Adam did in the garden: “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit of the tree, and I ate” (Genesis 3:12). We recruit allies, post online, threaten to resign or to leave. At its worst, attack becomes intimidation or violence, like King Saul hurling his spear at David (1 Samuel 18:11).

This is peace-breaking. Paul warned a church that was turning on itself: “But if you bite and devour one another, watch out that you are not consumed by one another” (Galatians 5:15). Winning an argument can cost a marriage, a friendship or a church.

Quieter attacks

Not every attack is loud. Some people never raise their voice, yet punish with a cold silence, a pointed absence or a polite email copied to the boss. David described a man like that: “His speech was smooth as butter, yet war was in his heart” (Psalm 55:21). Passive aggression is still aggression.

Why both feel right

Each reflex has a good instinct buried in it. The one who runs wants peace and hates hurting people. The one who fights wants truth and hates injustice. Those are good desires. But escape gives up truth to keep a false peace, and attack gives up love to win a point. The biblical way, which we will see in later chapters, refuses both trades. It is “speaking the truth in love” (Ephesians 4:15).

Many of us do both

The reflexes often take turns. A man keeps quiet about his frustrations for months, and then one small thing sets off an explosion that shocks everyone, including him. A woman fights hard at work, where she feels she must, and avoids every hard conversation at home. Knowing your own pattern, and when it changes, is an important step.

A word of care

For some people, the urge to escape a painful situation becomes overwhelming. If you ever find yourself thinking of harming yourself or ending your life to get away from it all, please get help now. Call the emergency services (999 or 112 in the UK and Europe, 911 in North America) or a crisis line (Samaritans on 116 123 in the UK and Ireland, 988 in the United States), and tell someone you trust. No conflict is worth your life, and your life is precious to God.

An example

A couple married for fifteen years describe their arguments the same way. He goes silent and leaves the room. She follows him, raising her voice, because his silence feels like rejection. The more she pursues, the more he withdraws; the more he withdraws, the louder she gets. Each thinks the other is the problem. It takes a wise friend to show them that they are caught in the same dance, one running and one fighting, and that neither step leads anywhere good.

For reflection

Which reflex comes most naturally to you, running away or hitting back? Which forms of it do you recognise in yourself? Who do you tend to talk to about a conflict instead of talking to the person involved? What good desire might be hidden inside your usual reflex?

3.title: What Lies Beneath the Quarrel
3.essay:
We usually explain our conflicts by pointing at the other person. They are unreasonable, selfish, careless or rude. Sometimes that is true. But the Bible asks a harder and more hopeful question: what is going on in me?

The war inside

James goes straight to the root. “What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you? You desire and do not have, so you murder. You covet and cannot obtain, so you fight and quarrel” (James 4:1–2).

The fight on the outside begins with a fight on the inside. James does not say that our desires are always wrong. Many are good: to be respected, to be listened to, to have a tidy home, a fair share of the work, a quiet evening, a church that sings the songs we love. The problem comes when a desire grows into a demand. “I would like” becomes “I must have”. Then anyone who stands in the way becomes an enemy.

How a desire takes over

The Christian writer Ken Sande, in his book The Peacemaker, traces how this happens. First I desire something. When I do not get it, the desire hardens into a demand. Then I judge the person who is withholding it: they are selfish, they do not care. And finally I punish them, with harsh words, a cold shoulder or a hundred small ways of making them pay. By then the desire is ruling me. It has become what the Bible calls an idol.

A useful question in any conflict is this: what do I want so badly that I am willing to sin to get it, or sin because I cannot have it? Usually the honest answer is surprisingly small: being right, being thanked, getting my way about a holiday.

“You do not ask”

James adds something we easily miss: “You do not have, because you do not ask. You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, to spend it on your passions” (James 4:2–3). Many conflicts are fought hard on earth and never once brought to God. We try to win from people what we have not asked from our Father. Or we pray, but only for the other person to change so that we can have what we want. Prayer that hands our desires over to God, and asks him to reorder them, takes the heat out of a great many quarrels.

Under the running: fear

Why do some of us run? Often because we are afraid: of the other person’s anger, of being disliked, of losing a job, a friendship or our place in the church. “The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe” (Proverbs 29:25). When people’s approval has become what we cannot live without, we will do almost anything to avoid displeasing them, including leaving wrongs unspoken and problems unsolved. The study The Fear of Man explores this in depth.

Under the fighting: pride

Why do some of us fight? Often because of pride. “By insolence comes nothing but strife, but with those who take advice is wisdom” (Proverbs 13:10). Pride needs to be right, to have the last word, to be seen to win. It cannot bear being corrected, especially in front of others. It rarely asks, “Could I be wrong?” The disciples argued at the Last Supper over “which of them was to be regarded as the greatest” (Luke 22:24), on the very night their Lord was about to die for them. Pride is a stubborn root. The study Humility & Pride says more.

One root, two shoots

Fear and pride look like opposites, but notice something in Proverbs. “A greedy man stirs up strife, but the one who trusts in the LORD will be enriched” (Proverbs 28:25). And again, the fear of man is a snare, but “whoever trusts in the LORD is safe” (Proverbs 29:25). In both proverbs the opposite of the problem is the same: trust in the LORD. Whether we run or fight, we are trying to secure for ourselves what we do not believe God will give us: safety, respect, fairness, our own way. At bottom, conflict exposes what we are trusting.

Looking inside is a mercy

This could feel crushing. It is meant to free us. If the problem were only the other person, we would be helpless until they changed. But if part of the problem is in us, then God can begin his work right now, in the one heart we can bring to him. He is the God who gives “more grace” (James 4:6) to the humble.

An example

A man is furious with his brother over their mother’s care. He believes he does all the visiting while his brother does nothing. Talking with his pastor, he is asked what he wants most. He starts with “fairness”, but after a while admits something deeper: he wants his mother, and his brother, to finally see how much he does. That desire is understandable. But it has been running his life, and every family meal has become a courtroom. He begins to pray about it honestly for the first time.

For reflection

Think of a current or recent conflict. What did you want? When did that desire become a demand? Is your usual reflex driven more by fear or by pride? Have you brought this conflict to God in prayer, asking him to change you as well as the other person? What would it look like to trust the Lord for what you have been fighting, or hiding, to secure?

4.title: The God Who Came to Make Peace
4.essay:
Before the Bible tells us how to make peace, it shows us a God who has made it. The greatest conflict in history was not between nations or families. It was between the holy God and his rebellious creatures. And the way he handled it changes everything about how we handle ours.

The deepest conflict

Scripture does not soften our condition. We were not merely distant from God. We were his enemies, “alienated and hostile in mind, doing evil deeds” (Colossians 1:21). The fault was entirely ours. God had every right to be done with us.

Think of the two reflexes from earlier in this study. God could have run from the conflict: ignored our sin, pretended all was well, healed the wound lightly. But a holy God cannot fake peace. Or he could have attacked: given us exactly what our rebellion deserved. That would have been just. But it would have been the end of us.

He did neither. He came.

God took the first step

“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). And again: “For if while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, now that we are reconciled, shall we be saved by his life” (Romans 5:10). God did not wait for us to apologise. He did not demand that we meet him halfway. The offended party crossed the whole distance.

Paul says, “All this is from God, who through Christ reconciled us to himself” (2 Corinthians 5:18). In ordinary conflicts we expect the one in the wrong to make the first move. In the gospel, the one who was wronged moves first.

Peace at a price

This was not peace-faking. God did not overlook our sin. He dealt with it fully, by laying it on his Son. “He was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace” (Isaiah 53:5). The truth about our sin was not hidden; it was judged. And love was not set aside; it paid the price. At the cross, truth and love meet completely. Christ made peace “by the blood of his cross” (Colossians 1:20).

That is the third way that every peacemaker is reaching for: neither escape nor attack, but costly love that takes the wrong seriously and still moves towards the other person. We can only reach for it because God did it first, and did it for us.

The hostility killed

The cross also makes peace between people. In Paul’s day the deepest human division ran between Jews and Gentiles. Yet Paul writes that Christ “himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility … that he might create in himself one new man in place of the two, so making peace, and might reconcile us both to God in one body through the cross, thereby killing the hostility” (Ephesians 2:14–16).

Notice the words “killing the hostility”. When two Christians are in conflict, they are two people for whom the same Saviour died, two members of one body. The hostility between them has already been put to death at the cross. Their task is not to create a peace that does not exist, but to live out a peace Christ has already won. That is why the New Testament can say, “let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, to which indeed you were called in one body” (Colossians 3:15).

Ambassadors and children

Those who have been reconciled are given a job. God “gave us the ministry of reconciliation” (2 Corinthians 5:18), and “we are ambassadors for Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:20). That ministry is first the message of peace with God, but it shapes every relationship. A Christian walking into a hard conversation carries a peace that is not their own.

And Jesus says, “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5:9). Children resemble their father. When we move towards someone in love to make peace, we look like the God who moved towards us. There is no higher family likeness than that.

Jesus at the table

Remember the argument at the Last Supper over who was the greatest. Jesus did not ignore it, and he did not shout them down. He answered gently: “let the greatest among you become as the youngest, and the leader as one who serves … I am among you as the one who serves” (Luke 22:26–27). Within hours he would serve them to the uttermost, giving his life for the very men who had been squabbling over status. This is our Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6). He does not only teach peacemaking. He is peace, for us.

The study Forgiveness & Reconciliation explores more fully what it means to be reconciled to God.

An example

A woman has been at odds with her elderly father for years. She has always believed that since he hurt her, he must make the first move. One Good Friday, hearing Romans 5:8 read aloud, she is struck that God did not wait for her. She does not pretend the past did not happen. But she writes to her father, simply and honestly, saying she would like to talk. It is the first step in a long road, and she takes it because someone took the first step towards her.

For reflection

How did God handle the conflict between himself and us? What does that show you about the two reflexes, escape and attack? What difference does it make to know that the hostility between Christians has already been killed at the cross? Is there someone towards whom you need to take the first step, even though you were the one wronged?

5.title: The Peacemaker’s Way
5.essay:
The gospel does not only give us a reason to make peace. Through Jesus, Paul and the wisdom of Proverbs, it gives us a way. It begins, surprisingly, with ourselves.

The log comes first

Jesus asks a question that is almost funny. “Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but do not notice the log that is in your own eye?” (Matthew 7:3). Picture someone with a plank sticking out of their face, offering to help with a speck of dust in someone else’s. Then the command: “You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother’s eye” (Matthew 7:5).

Jesus does not say the speck does not matter. He says we will not see it clearly until we have dealt with our own part. And our part usually looks bigger once we look honestly. It may be a sharp tone, an assumption, a delay, a broken promise, a sulk, a story told about them to others. Even if the other person is ninety per cent to blame, the ten per cent that is ours is the part we can deal with today.

Owning our part does not mean taking all the blame, or saying we were wrong when we were not. It means confessing specifically, without excuses, what we did. Few things disarm a conflict faster than “I was wrong to speak to you like that.”

Overlook, or go

Once our own eye is clearer, we face a choice. Many offences can simply be covered. “Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all offenses” (Proverbs 10:12). Isaac’s herdsmen were driven from one well, then another, and Isaac simply moved and dug again, until he could say, “For now the LORD has made room for us” (Genesis 26:22). Letting it go can be strength, not weakness.

But some things cannot be covered: when a pattern is harming someone, when the relationship is cooling because of it, when the matter is serious. Then Jesus says, “If your brother sins against you, go and tell him his fault, between you and him alone” (Matthew 18:15). Notice three things. Go: do not wait for them to come to you. Between you and him alone: not in front of others, not by hints, not online. And the goal: “If he listens to you, you have gained your brother” (Matthew 18:15). The aim is not to win the argument but to win the person.

Gentle, and watchful

Paul adds the spirit in which we go. “Brothers, if anyone is caught in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness. Keep watch on yourself, lest you too be tempted” (Galatians 6:1). The word translated restore could be used of setting a broken bone. It is careful work, done with gentle hands. And the one who restores stays humble, aware of his own weakness.

The power of a soft answer

Proverbs is full of practical wisdom about tone. “A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger” (Proverbs 15:1). “A hot-tempered man stirs up strife, but he who is slow to anger quiets contention” (Proverbs 15:18). And this striking picture: “With patience a ruler may be persuaded, and a soft tongue will break a bone” (Proverbs 25:15). Gentleness is not weakness. A calm, patient word can break through resistance that shouting only hardens.

Proverbs also tells us when to act: “The beginning of strife is like letting out water, so quit before the quarrel breaks out” (Proverbs 17:14). A small leak in a dam is easy to stop; a flood is not. Deal with things early.

Truth without aggression or fear

Peacemaking is not the same as being nice. Sometimes we must say something hard. When an officer struck Jesus at his trial, Jesus did not lash out, and he did not cower. He said, “If what I said is wrong, bear witness about the wrong; but if what I said is right, why do you strike me?” (John 18:23). That is truth spoken calmly, with no aggression and no fear. It is possible only for someone secure in his Father’s love. In Christ, that security is ours too. The study The Tongue has a chapter on speaking the truth in love.

Abigail, peacemaker

One of the finest peacemakers in Scripture is a woman in a hard marriage. Her husband Nabal was “harsh and badly behaved” (1 Samuel 25:3). When David’s men, who had protected Nabal’s flocks, asked for food, Nabal insulted them. David, furious, set out with four hundred men to destroy the household.

Abigail did not run, and she did not take up arms. She moved quickly. She brought a generous gift. She met David on the road, humbled herself and said, “On me alone, my lord, be the guilt” (1 Samuel 25:24), taking the blame she did not deserve. Then she spoke truth to David’s conscience: if he went ahead, he would have “cause of grief or pangs of conscience for having shed blood without cause” (1 Samuel 25:31). And she pointed him to God’s promises for his future.

David listened. “Blessed be your discretion, and blessed be you, who have kept me this day from bloodguilt” (1 Samuel 25:33). One wise, humble, courageous person turned back an army. And in her standing between an angry king and a guilty household, taking the guilt on herself, we catch a faint picture of a far greater Mediator.

An example

A church treasurer is convinced that one of the elders has been careless with the accounts. For weeks he grumbles to his wife. Then he reads Matthew 7 and realises his own log: he has not kept the elder informed, and he has been quick to assume the worst. He asks the elder for coffee, admits his part first, and then gently explains his concern. The elder is relieved to hear it plainly. Together they find the problem, which turns out to be a simple misunderstanding.

For reflection

In a conflict you are facing, what is your log? How would you describe your part honestly and specifically? Is this an offence to overlook or one to go and speak about privately? Which of the proverbs in this chapter do you most need? What strikes you most about Abigail, and what would it look like to follow her example?

6.title: Before, During and After the Hard Conversation
6.essay:
Most of us know what we ought to do. What we lack is courage, and some wisdom for the moment itself. Here is practical help, offered not as a technique for getting our way, but as ways to love the other person and honour Christ when tensions are high.

Before: prepare

Pray first. Bring your desires to God, ask him to show you your part, and pray for the other person by name. It is hard to stay hostile towards someone you are honestly praying for.

Get clear. Write down what happened, what you felt, what your part was and what you are hoping for. Separate facts from assumptions. Aim for one issue, not a list of grievances going back years.

Choose the time and place. “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in a setting of silver” (Proverbs 25:11). Do not start a serious conversation late at night, when someone is hungry or rushing out, or in front of others. Hard things are best said face to face, not by text or email, where tone is easily misread. Abigail waited until morning to tell Nabal what had happened, when he was sober enough to hear it (1 Samuel 25:37).

During: listen first

“If one gives an answer before he hears, it is his folly and shame” (Proverbs 18:13). Let the other person speak. Ask questions to understand, not to trap. “The purpose in a man’s heart is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out” (Proverbs 20:5). Try repeating back what you heard: “So you felt I ignored your idea in the meeting. Is that right?” Remember too that “The one who states his case first seems right, until the other comes and examines him” (Proverbs 18:17). You may be missing part of the story.

During: speak carefully

Own your part first, specifically and without excuses.

Describe, do not accuse. Speak about what happened and how it affected you, rather than labelling the other person. “When the plan changed without warning, I felt sidelined” is easier to hear than “You never respect me.” Words like “always” and “never” are rarely true and almost always inflame.

Look for the shared ground. Euodia and Syntyche were urged to agree “in the Lord” (Philippians 4:2). What do you both want? Often it is the same thing: the children cared for, the project done well, the church healthy.

Take a pause if needed. If voices are rising, it is wise to say, “Can we stop and come back to this tomorrow?” and then actually come back. The study Anger has more help for when your temper is the problem.

When to involve others

If a private conversation fails over a serious matter, Jesus says, “take one or two others along with you” (Matthew 18:16). Paul asked a “true companion” to help Euodia and Syntyche (Philippians 4:3). A wise, trusted friend, a pastor or elder, or a trained mediator can help two people hear each other. Between believers, serious disputes should if possible be settled within the church rather than in the courts (1 Corinthians 6:5–7), though legal protection may be needed where someone refuses correction.

Involving others is different from recruiting allies. Bring in people to help, not to take your side.

Conflict at work

A difficult boss is a particular trial. Scripture calls for respect, “not only to the good and gentle but also to the unjust” (1 Peter 2:18). That does not mean silence. “If the anger of the ruler rises against you, do not leave your place, for calmness will lay great offenses to rest” (Ecclesiastes 10:4). Daniel, asked to do something against his conscience, did not rebel; he respectfully proposed an alternative and asked for a ten-day trial (Daniel 1:8–13). Raise concerns calmly, privately and with facts. Use the proper channels, and keep a record where things are serious. If you are asked to do something wrong or unsafe, you must refuse, and report it if necessary. Sometimes, after much prayer and advice, the right step is to look for another job. The study Christian at Work says more about life at work.

When the other will not make peace

“If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all” (Romans 12:18). You are responsible for your part, not theirs. You can pray, go humbly, own your wrongs, and leave the door open. You cannot force someone to reconcile. If they refuse, do not repay evil for evil, keep blessing them, and leave the outcome with God. The study Forgiveness & Reconciliation covers forgiving, rebuilding trust and the long road afterwards.

Abuse is not “conflict”

Conflict is a clash between two people who both have a voice. Abuse is different: one person using power to control, frighten or harm another. It may be physical, sexual, emotional, verbal or financial. In abuse, the advice of this study, go privately, own your part, meet together, does not apply, and can put someone in danger. Abuse is never acceptable.

If you are being abused, your safety comes first. Get to a safe place, tell someone you trust, and contact the police or a domestic abuse helpline. In immediate danger, call the emergency services (999 or 112 in the UK and Europe, 911 in North America). Abuse must be reported, and church leaders should support the person harmed, not press them to “sort it out”. Leaving to escape abuse is not a failure of faith. The study Divorce & Remarriage says more.

Afterwards

Even a good conversation can leave you shaken. Give thanks for any progress, however small. If it went badly, bring it to God rather than replaying it all night, and ask whether there is anything you need to put right. If conflict leaves you persistently anxious, low or unable to sleep, talk to a doctor or a qualified counsellor. That is no failure of faith.

An example

An office worker’s manager keeps criticising her in team meetings. She prays, writes down three specific examples, and asks for a private meeting at the start of the day. She begins by acknowledging a missed deadline of her own. Then she calmly explains how the public criticism affects her, and asks whether concerns could be raised with her directly. Her manager is surprised, a little defensive, but agrees. Things are not perfect, but they are better, and she has spoken without fear and without attack.

For reflection

Is there a hard conversation you need to prepare for? What time and place would be wise? Which part of listening or speaking do you find hardest? Is there a situation where you have done all that depends on you, and now need to leave it with God?
